sections.b: Proverbs ends with an alphabet poem of twenty-two lines (31:10–31). The woman of strength looks for wool and flax, trades like a merchant ship, rises before dawn to feed her household, buys a field and plants a vineyard, makes cloth to wear and to sell, opens her hand to the poor and speaks with wisdom and "the teaching of loyal love" (31:26). Her husband trusts her and is honored at the gate; her sons call her happy; her husband says she has "climbed above them all" (31:29). Her secret is named last: "A woman who fears the LORD, she is the one to be praised" (31:30). The poem uses the language of hero songs: plunder, prey, might tied on like a belt (31:11, 15, 17). The word chayil also links her to the queen mother's warning not to give a king's strength to women (31:3).

Readers have seen more than a wife in her. Many scholars read her as Wisdom in human form, closing a book that opened with Lady Wisdom (Proverbs 1:20–33; 8–9). Midrash Mishlei read her as the Torah and her verses as the righteous women of Israel, from Sarah to Ruth. Kabbalists saw the Shekhinah and began the custom of singing the poem on Friday evening. Augustine preached on her as the church (Sermon 37), and medieval writers saw Mary. Since the Reformation she has usually been read as an ideal Christian wife, and today she is claimed by both complementarians and egalitarians in debates about women's roles.

common: Proverbs 31:10–31 describes the ideal wife and mother.
The poem's final praise rests on her fear of the LORD, not her beauty or busyness (31:30).
uncommon: The poem is a heroic hymn in the style of songs for warriors (Wolters).
The tsade line's tsofiyyah is a pun on the Greek sophia, naming her Wisdom (Wolters).

sections.b: Agur says he is more beast than man and has not learned wisdom (Proverbs 30:2–3). He asks who has gone up to heaven and come down, collected the wind, bundled up the waters and set the ends of the earth, and "what is his son's name?" (30:4). His answer is God's tested word (30:5–6), and his prayer asks for neither poverty nor riches but "the bread that is my share" (30:8). Whether 30:1 names Ithiel and Ucal or cries "I am weary, God" is debated, and the Greek and Latin read words there, not names.

The words of Lemuel are his mother's: what she "disciplined him" with (Proverbs 31:1). She warns him not to give his strength to women or his judgment to wine, and charges him, "Open your mouth for the one who cannot speak" (31:8). It is the only teaching in Proverbs given in a mother's own words, and the poem of the woman of strength follows it.

sections.h: Proverbs 30: things never satisfied, too wonderful, unbearable, small and stately
sections.b: The numerical sayings of Proverbs 30 count four sets. First come things that never say "Plenty!": Sheol, the closed-up womb, dry land and fire (30:15–16). Next come ways too wonderful to know: an eagle, a snake, a ship, and a man with a young woman (30:18–19). Then come things the earth cannot bear: a slave made king, a fool well fed, an unloved woman married, and a slave woman replacing her mistress (30:21–23). Last come creatures that walk with a fine stride: the lion, the rooster, the billy goat and a king (30:29–31). Between them stands a plain list of four small, wise animals (30:24–28). The Greek moves the whole block (30:15–33) to follow 24:34.

common: The last item in a numerical list is usually the one that matters most.

sections.b: Lemuel's mother tells her son, "It is not for kings, Lemuel, / not for kings to drink wine", because a drinking ruler may "forget what the law says, / and twist the case of all the afflicted" (Proverbs 31:4–5). Then she says, "Give beer to someone who is perishing, / and wine to those who are bitter in spirit" (31:6). The Talmud cites the verse for the drugged wine given to condemned men (Bavli Sanhedrin 43a), and Mark tells how Jesus refused wine mixed with myrrh on the cross (Mark 15:23). The Assemblies of God cites these verses for total abstinence. The Southern Baptist Convention's 2006 resolution asked that its leaders not drink. Churches that practice moderation read the passage as a warning about judgment, not a ban.

sections.h: The woman of strength and women's roles
sections.b: Proverbs 31:10–31 is often cited in debates about women's roles, though it does not mention worship or church office. Complementarians see a wife whose wide work serves her household. Egalitarians point out that she buys land, trades, manages workers and teaches "the teaching of loyal love" (Proverbs 31:16, 24, 26), so the Bible praises women's public competence. The poem also gives the only mother's teaching in Proverbs (31:1–9).

The poem of the woman of strength runs from alef ('eshet, "a woman", Proverbs 31:10) to tav (tenu, "give", 31:31), one verse per letter. It puts ayin before pe, the usual order, as Lamentations 1 does, while Lamentations 2, 3 and 4 put pe first. The tsade verse opens with the unusual tsofiyyah, "keeping watch" (31:27), which may be a pun on Greek sophia. The Greek translation, which moves the poem to follow 29:27, does not keep the alphabet. It also reverses 31:25 and 31:26, so its lines would run pe before ayin, the order of Lamentations 2–4. Whether the translator's Hebrew had that order is not known.

sections.h: Agur: wisdom that admits its limits
sections.b: Near the end of Proverbs a sage confesses, "I have not learned wisdom" (Proverbs 30:3), and asks who has gone up to heaven (30:4). The answer he gives is God's word, "refined like metal" (30:5). The book that praised wisdom ends by placing it under revelation and the fear of the LORD (31:30), and the woman of strength, worth more than red coral like Wisdom herself (3:15; 31:10), shows wisdom lived in a household.

sections.h: The last collections: Agur, Lemuel and the woman of strength
sections.b: Proverbs 30–31 holds three short collections with their own headings: the words of Agur (30), the words of Lemuel, taught him by his mother (31:1–9), and the alphabet poem of the woman of strength (31:10–31). In the Greek these pieces are scattered: 30:1–14 after 24:22, 30:15–33 after 24:34, 31:1–9 next, and 31:10–31 after 29:27, with the names Agur and Lemuel turned into words. No Dead Sea Scroll preserves these chapters.

sections.h: Ruth and the woman of strength
sections.b: Boaz tells Ruth, "the whole town knows that you are a woman of worth" (Ruth 3:11), the same Hebrew phrase as the woman of strength in Proverbs 31:10. In the Leningrad Codex Ruth follows Proverbs directly. Midrash Mishlei assigns Proverbs 31:29, "you have climbed above them all", to Ruth.

Agur asks of the one who rules wind and water, "What is his name, and what is his son's name?" (Proverbs 30:4). Readers have answered Israel (Exodus 4:22), a human expert, Moses (Rashi) or the eternal Son (Augustine; Matthew Henry). The Greek has "his children". Christian readers often set the verse beside John 3:13.

Agur quotes a psalm, "Every saying of God is refined like metal" (Proverbs 30:5; Psalm 18:30), and warns, "Add nothing to his words" (Proverbs 30:6), echoing Deuteronomy 4:2. These two verses are among the clearest places where Proverbs appeals to written revelation.

sections.h: Do not add to his words (Proverbs 30:6)
sections.b: Proverbs 30:6 repeats the warning of Deuteronomy 4:2 and 12:32 against adding to God's words, a warning Revelation 22:18–19 applies to its own book. Some scholars take Proverbs 30:5–6 as evidence that a body of Scripture already had special authority when the last parts of Proverbs were added.

sections.h: The poor at the end of Proverbs
sections.b: The last chapters keep returning to the poor: a generation that devours them (Proverbs 30:14), a king told to "take up the case of the poor and the needy" (31:9), and a woman who "spreads her palm open to the poor" (31:20). Agur prays not to be poor, lest he steal (30:9).

Agur asks, "Do not give me poverty or riches. / Feed me with the bread that is my share" (Proverbs 30:8), because the full may deny God and the poor may steal (30:9). The prayer is often read beside the Lord's Prayer for daily bread (Matthew 6:11) and Paul's contentment (Philippians 4:11–12).
Agur's "Two things I ask from you" (Proverbs 30:7–9) is the one prayer in the book: keep falsehood far away, and give neither poverty nor riches.

sections.h: "Open your mouth for the one who cannot speak"
sections.b: Lemuel's mother defines the king's work as speaking for the voiceless and judging the poor rightly (Proverbs 31:8–9), the ideal of Psalm 72 and of Jeremiah's praise of Josiah (Jeremiah 22:15–16).
A king's mother warns him against many women and strong drink and charges him to judge for the poor (Proverbs 31:1–9), the same dangers the law of the king names (Deuteronomy 17:17).
Sheol heads the list of things that never say "Plenty!", beside the closed-up womb, thirsty land and fire (Proverbs 30:15–16; compare Proverbs 27:20 and Habakkuk 2:5).

The woman of strength has torat chesed on her tongue (Proverbs 31:26), "the teaching of loyal love", teaching marked by loyal love. Ruth, whom Boaz calls a woman of worth, is praised for the same chesed (Ruth 3:10–11).

In the poem of the woman of strength, the husband's part is to trust her (Proverbs 31:11), to be known at the gates (31:23) and to praise her (31:28–29). Proverbs had already said that a woman of strength is "her husband's crown" (12:4) and a sensible wife a gift from the LORD (19:14).

sections.h: Who has set the ends of the earth? (Proverbs 30:4)
sections.b: Agur's questions about wind, waters and the ends of the earth (Proverbs 30:4) belong with Job 38 and Isaiah 40:12: only the Creator holds the world in his hands.

sections.h: Numerical sayings and a world turned upside down
sections.b: The "three... four" sayings of Proverbs 30 have older relatives in a Ugaritic poem (KTU 1.4 iii 17–21) and in the Aramaic Story of Ahiqar, and the upside-down world of Proverbs 30:21–23 recalls the Egyptian Admonitions of Ipuwer.

Proverbs 30:10 forbids slandering a servant to his master. The Greek has "do not hand a servant over to a master", like Deuteronomy 23:15. Proverbs 30:22–23 counts a slave made king and a slave woman replacing her mistress among the things the earth cannot bear. It is a view of the social order from above.
